statement: For decoder-only language models below 100M parameters, the loss-optimal learning-rate warmdown fraction is approximately 33% of the training run, and this optimum is stable across model size, precision, optimizer and schedule shape.

scope.budget: from-initialisation training; the cited grids vary training length up to 9x

locators.location: abstract, arXiv 2605.25966v1, retrieved verbatim from the arXiv Atom API
locators.excerpt: A 720-run factorial grid (Phase 2) over bit-width x warmdown fraction x LR magnitude x model size x seed (FP16/INT8/INT6, 15M-100M, 5 seeds) finds the optimal warmdown is 33% at every (bit-width, size) cell. ... A 625-run follow-up (Phase 5) probes the null along five axes: optimiser (AdamW), schedule shape (cosine), training length (up to 9x more iterations), an extended size sweep (5M-350M), and an INT4 sweep from 3M to 100M. The null is robust under all three setup changes.

metrics.name: optimal_warmdown_fraction
metrics.result: 33%, invariant across bit-width and size in a 720-run grid, and robust in a 625-run follow-up varying optimizer, schedule shape and training length. The campaign's active baseline uses WARMDOWN_RATIO = 0.5.

assessment.rationale: Directness is direct: the paper varies warmdown fraction explicitly and reports an optimum, and our model at 50.33M sits inside its 15M-100M primary grid, so this is a within-range read rather than an extrapolation. Scope match is close rather than exact for two reasons that matter. First, the paper's frame is quantisation-aware training and its headline question is whether bit-width changes the optimum; the 33% figure is the shared optimum it reports across cells including FP16, which is our regime, but it was not a study designed around FP16/bf16 alone. Second, and more importantly, the paper's budget is a fixed ITERATION count while ours is a fixed 300 charged SECONDS, so our step count is not known in advance and varied 613-698 across three identical controls. A warmdown fraction defined over an unknown horizon is not the same quantity the paper optimised. Our schedule is time-parameterised (progress = training_time / TIME_BUDGET), which makes the transfer plausible but not automatic. Risk of bias medium: abstract only, no artifact inspected, single group. This is strong enough to justify one cheap knob test and not strong enough to adopt without measuring.
